rows.evidence: Q1: Sections 3-4 - authors run a distributed hydrological model (Tetis) for 1994-2015 over the Plana de Valencia Sur with 100 Monte Carlo parameter sets, calibrated against observed evaporative index, groundwater levels from four wells and soil moisture. Q2: Section 4.2 and Figure 6 - mean annual recharge for flood irrigation (231 mm) exceeded drip irrigation (210 mm) by about 21 mm (~10%), with flood recharge higher in 16 of 20 years; model output was compared with groundwater level observations from four wells inside the study area (Figure 4) and with field evaporative index estimates (Figure 3), so the simulation is checked against measurements from the real system. Q4: Section 4.2, Figures 5, 7b and 8 - the model simulates soil water storage under wet/dry drip pixels and flood pixels, and shows that recharge in flood-irrigated areas also occurs on non-rainy days (i.e., from irrigation return flow) and that during the flood-irrigation season (March-September) flood areas produced 68 mm more cumulative recharge than drip areas; Section 5.1 attributes the difference to soil moisture status produced by the irrigation schedule. Q6: Section 2 and 3.3.3 - results are aggregated over 68 irrigation sectors covering ~382 km2 of irrigated land within a 913 km2 modeled area, i.e., basin/regional scale. Q8: Section 5.2 - splitting drip sectors into wet/dry pixels limits interpretation to sector scale and translating plot-scale wetting to 200 m pixels is a strong simplification; Section 5.3 - no split-sample validation possible, increasing uncertainty of absolute recharge values; soil moisture data came from outside the modeled area; short discontinuous time series; Section 6 - findings limited to the Mediterranean region. Q9: Figure 6 boxplots and Figure 7 points show the spread of the 12 accepted parameterizations for annual recharge in flood and drip; cumulative recharge plotted with median, minimum and maximum of the 12 parameterizations; Section 4.2 reports ranges (drip 84-343 mm, flood 132-338 mm); Table 2 gives standard errors of regression coefficients including drip-irrigated area (-0.287, SE 0.084).
rows.notes: Q3 no: a single method (one calibrated hydrological model); the multiple calibration datasets constrain the same model rather than independently estimating the recharge difference. Q5 no: one region, one climate, essentially one crop (citrus orchards). Q7 doubtful: the authors show that flood recharge exceeds drip mainly in below-average rainfall years and during the irrigation season, and that drip can exceed flood in wet years and in autumn/winter, but this is presented as a correlation/gradient (Spearman -0.83 with annual precipitation) rather than an explicitly stated requirement, so marked no. Note the study also finds annual precipitation has roughly four times more influence on recharge than irrigation practice, and that the direction of the difference reverses in wet years, which qualifies the generality of the claim.

notes: Full text appears complete (abstract through references). The study is a basin-scale modeling study with multi-objective calibration against field observations; the recharge difference between flood and drip is a simulated quantity, not directly measured.
